birth_prophet.title: Birth of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ
birth_prophet.dateLabel: Around 570–571 CE (Year of the Elephant; approximate conversion)
birth_prophet.summary: Muhammad ﷺ was born in Makkah among the Banu Hashim of Quraysh. The biographical tradition places his birth in the Year of the Elephant, around 570–571 CE; Monday is reported in Sahih Muslim, while the exact month and day remain disputed. According to the most widespread biographical account, his father ʿAbd Allah had already died, and his mother Aminah cared for him in his earliest days.

content.heading: Context and setting
content.body: Makkah was a pilgrimage centre around the Kaʿbah and a place of exchange among western Arabian tribes. Muhammad ﷺ belonged to Banu Hashim, a branch of Quraysh. According to the most widespread biographical account, his father ʿAbd Allah had already died, and his mother Aminah cared for him in his earliest days.

content.heading: Narrative and sequence
content.body: Early biographies connect his birth with the Year of the Elephant. Authors do not agree on the exact day of Rabiʿ al-Awwal, nor is a precise conversion to the Gregorian calendar certain. The hadith of Abu Qatadah reports the Prophet ﷺ saying that he was born on a Monday; it does not state the month, day of the month or year. Monday should therefore be retained as the explicitly reported detail, while the year remains an approximate traditional chronology.

content.heading: Significance and lessons
content.body: This birth begins the account of the Prophet’s ﷺ life. His early years were marked by the early loss of his father, care by his family and nursing among Banu Saʿd. These details belong to transmitted biographical reports and should be distinguished from an explicitly identified hadith.

content.heading: Sources and strength of evidence
content.body: Targeted reference: Sahih Muslim, 1162e · Livre du jeûne, 13, hadith 256. This hadith establishes Monday as the day of birth. It does not specify the month or day of the month. This reference supports only the elements it explicitly reports; it is not, by itself, a complete chronology of the episode.

birth_prophet.reliabilityNote: Sahih Muslim 1162e reports Monday, without specifying month, day or year. The Year of the Elephant and family context come from the Seerah tradition, particularly Ibn Ishaq as transmitted by Ibn Hisham. The Islamic Academy of Coventry synthesis (Sīrah of Muhammad, Part 3, 2nd ed., 2023, p. 8) also notes the lack of agreement on the exact day. Do not present a traditional date as certain.

abdullah_death.title: Death of Abdullah, the Prophet's ﷺ father
abdullah_death.dateLabel: Before or shortly after the birth
abdullah_death.summary: ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib died while Aminah was pregnant or shortly after the birth, according to differing biographical reports. The most widespread account places his death in Yathrib, where he had stayed ill after a journey. Seerah accounts describe him travelling north with a trading caravan. This entry preserves the chronological disagreement rather than imposing one exact date or scenario.

content.heading: Context and setting
content.body: ʿAbd Allah was the son of ʿAbd al-Muttalib and the husband of Aminah bint Wahb. Seerah accounts describe him travelling north with a trading caravan. On the return journey, he remained in Yathrib with maternal relatives or close family, while the caravan continued to Makkah.

content.heading: Narrative and sequence
content.body: In the most commonly transmitted version, ʿAbd Allah became ill in Yathrib and died there before his son was born. Some chronologies, however, report that he died shortly after the birth. The Islamic Academy of Coventry synthesis follows the first version and places his death in Yathrib. This entry preserves the chronological disagreement rather than imposing one exact date or scenario.

content.heading: Significance and lessons
content.body: According to the majority account, Muhammad ﷺ was therefore born without his father. His paternal family, especially his grandfather ʿAbd al-Muttalib, then played an essential role in his care. This early orphanhood is an important feature of his childhood. Within the Sīrah sequence, this episode is illuminated by what comes before and after it. It prepares the reader for “Nursing among the Banu Sa'd” and shows how decisions, family ties, journeys and places connect across the narrative. This is a reading aid, not an independent new proof.

halimah_nursing.title: Nursing among the Banu Sa'd
halimah_nursing.summary: In the biographical tradition, Muhammad ﷺ was entrusted to Halimah al-Saʿdiyyah, a wet nurse from Banu Saʿd ibn Bakr. He spent part of his early childhood in a Bedouin setting around Makkah. Seerah biographies describe a practice in which Meccan families entrusted young children to wet nurses living in the desert.

content.heading: Context and setting
content.body: Seerah biographies describe a practice in which Meccan families entrusted young children to wet nurses living in the desert. A stay outside the city was associated with a different environment and learning Arabic among Bedouin tribes. Details of this custom are reported by Seerah authors and later summaries.

content.heading: Narrative and sequence
content.body: Halimah, from Banu Saʿd ibn Bakr, came to Makkah with her husband al-Harith to take a child into her care. The tradition says she accepted Muhammad ﷺ although he was fatherless. She then took him to live with her family among Banu Saʿd, in a region traditionally placed south-east of Makkah.

content.heading: Significance and lessons
content.body: This stay explains part of the Prophet’s ﷺ childhood and his ties with his milk family. It also offers a glimpse of wet-nursing practices and relations between Makkah and surrounding tribes. Exact ages and the duration of the stay vary among reports.

chest_opening.title: The purification of the heart
chest_opening.summary: Sahih Muslim reports from Anas ibn Malik an episode in which Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ as a child while he was playing with other boys, and his chest was opened and restored. The hadith does not specify an exact age. The report describes him being laid down, his chest being opened, a clot being removed, and his heart being washed in a vessel with water from Zamzam before being returned to its place.

content.heading: Context and setting
content.body: This episode belongs to the period “Birth and childhood”. It should be read within the family, social and geographical setting described by the accounts from this period. This context belongs to the “Birth and childhood” sequence. From the Prophet's ﷺ birth to his childhood with his guardians. It helps place the people and locations named in the wider setting of the period.

content.heading: Narrative and sequence
content.body: In Sahih Muslim 162c, Anas ibn Malik reports that Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was playing with companions. The report describes him being laid down, his chest being opened, a clot being removed, and his heart being washed in a vessel with water from Zamzam before being returned to its place. The other children then ran to his nurse, believing he had been killed.

content.heading: Significance and lessons
content.body: The episode has a place in accounts of the Prophet’s ﷺ childhood and connects Seerah tradition with a report included in Sahih Muslim. The exact content of the hadith must be distinguished from narrative elaborations in later biographies. Within the Sīrah sequence, this episode is illuminated by what comes before and after it. It prepares the reader for “Death of Aminah, the Prophet's ﷺ mother” and shows how decisions, family ties, journeys and places connect across the narrative. This is a reading aid, not an independent new proof.

content.heading: Place and chronology
content.body: The hadith places the episode in childhood and mentions playmates and the nurse, but gives no exact age, date or named geographical location. aminah_death.title: Death of Aminah, the Prophet's ﷺ mother
aminah_death.summary: According to the biographical tradition, Aminah bint Wahb died at al-Abwaʾ when Muhammad ﷺ was about six, while returning from a journey to Yathrib. Umm Ayman then brought him back to Makkah to his grandfather. The journey is linked to the maternal family and the memory of ʿAbd Allah, who according to the majority account had died in Yathrib.

content.heading: Context and setting
content.body: After his early years with Halimah and Banu Saʿd, Muhammad ﷺ lived again with his mother Aminah in Makkah. The tradition reports that she travelled with him to Yathrib, accompanied by Umm Ayman. The journey is linked to the maternal family and the memory of ʿAbd Allah, who according to the majority account had died in Yathrib.

content.heading: Narrative and sequence
content.body: On the return journey to Makkah, Aminah became ill and died at al-Abwaʾ, a place described in Seerah accounts between Yathrib and Makkah. Biographies usually place the event when the child was about six. The age and journey details belong to traditional chronology and should remain approximate.

content.heading: Significance and lessons
content.body: Aminah’s death meant that Muhammad ﷺ grew up without either parent. The account highlights the role of Umm Ayman and the paternal family in his care. Details from the biographical narrative should be distinguished from theological interpretations added by later authors.

guardianship.title: Guardianship of Abd al-Muttalib, then Abu Talib
guardianship.summary: Biographical accounts say that Abd al-Muttalib entrusted his grandson to Abu Talib before his own death. They place the grandfather’s death when Muhammad ﷺ was about eight; the exact age and its conversion to a Common Era year remain traditional chronological markers, not an absolute date.

content.heading: Context and setting
content.body: After Aminah’s death, Abd al-Muttalib took responsibility for the child. The biographical tradition describes his special affection for him and says that he appointed his son Abu Talib to continue his protection. Ibn Hisham includes this transfer in the account of Muhammad’s youth.

content.heading: Narrative and sequence
content.body: Abu Talib welcomed his nephew into his household and protected him. This family relationship later formed part of the social context in which Muhammad ﷺ began to proclaim the message in Makkah.

content.heading: Significance and lessons
content.body: Within the Sīrah sequence, this episode should be read alongside “The Prophet ﷺ as a shepherd”. It helps trace the changing circumstances of the community and the connections between the people and places named, without reducing the event to a date alone.

shepherd.title: The Prophet ﷺ as a shepherd
shepherd.summary: A report in Sahih al-Bukhari explicitly states that Muhammad ﷺ tended the sheep of the people of Makkah for payment. The report gives neither a precise period of his youth nor a particular grazing location. The text confirms the occupation and its connection with the people of Makkah.

content.heading: Context and setting
content.body: Abu Hurayra reports that the Prophet ﷺ said that prophets had tended sheep and that he himself tended the sheep of the people of Makkah for a few qirats. Reference: Sahih al-Bukhari 2262, Kitab al-Ijarah.

content.heading: Narrative and sequence
content.body: The text confirms the occupation and its connection with the people of Makkah. It names no valley, hill or owner. The app should therefore not display a specific pasture as though it were attested.

content.heading: Significance and lessons
content.body: The hadith connects this experience with a practice attributed to prophets. A spiritual reflection may draw lessons about responsibility and patience, but it must remain distinct from the hadith’s literal wording. Within the Sīrah sequence, this episode is illuminated by what comes before and after it. It prepares the reader for “Journey to Syria with Abu Talib” and shows how decisions, family ties, journeys and places connect across the narrative. syria_trip.title: Journey to Syria with Abu Talib
syria_trip.summary: Sirah biographies report a trading journey to al-Sham with his uncle Abu Talib when Muhammad ﷺ was young. The story of meeting the monk Bahira is well known, but its details and authenticity are debated; it should not be presented as a fact established by an unanimously authenticated hadith.

content.heading: Context and setting
content.body: The Sirah tradition places a journey to al-Sham within Quraysh’s caravan trade. Versions differ over the young Muhammad’s age and some details of the route. This context belongs to the “Youth and life before the revelation” sequence. The years of youth, trade, marriage and a reputation for honesty. It helps place the people and locations named in the wider setting of the period.

content.heading: Narrative and sequence
content.body: Some biographical reports associate the journey with a meeting with a monk named Bahira. The story has several forms and has been subject to critical discussion. It should be presented as a transmitted Sirah narrative, not as an event whose every detail is established.

content.heading: Significance and lessons

hilf_fudul.title: The Pact of the Fudul (Hilf al-Fudul)
hilf_fudul.summary: Sirah biographies describe the Hilf al-Fudul as a pact in Makkah to support wronged people regardless of their affiliation. The tradition says Muhammad ﷺ attended it before the revelation and later praised its principle. Accounts place it after the Fijar war, at the house of Abdullah ibn Jud‘an.

content.heading: Context and setting
content.body: Accounts place it after the Fijar war, at the house of Abdullah ibn Jud‘an. Several Quraysh clans are said to have pledged to support anyone wronged in Makkah until their right was restored.

content.heading: Narrative and sequence
content.body: The pact is presented as an effort to move beyond tribal solidarity when it shields wrongdoing. It is often described as a collective commitment to help the wronged, including visitors from outside the city.

content.heading: Significance and lessons
content.body: The tradition reports that the Prophet ﷺ later spoke favourably of the pact and said he would answer a similar call after Islam. The wording should be tied to the source consulted rather than presented as an unreferenced hadith. Within the Sīrah sequence, this episode is illuminated by what comes before and after it. It prepares the reader for “Marriage to Khadijah” and shows how decisions, family ties, journeys and places connect across the narrative. This is a reading aid, not an independent new proof.

marriage_khadijah.title: Marriage to Khadijah
marriage_khadijah.summary: Biographies place Muhammad’s ﷺ marriage to Khadijah bint Khuwaylid after the trading journey to al-Sham. They emphasise the trust placed in his work and Khadijah’s role as his first wife and major supporter. Some family and chronological details vary across reports. Biographical accounts describe Khadijah as a merchant who entrusted her goods to agents.

content.heading: Context and setting
content.body: Biographical accounts describe Khadijah as a merchant who entrusted her goods to agents. She is said to have offered Muhammad ﷺ a journey to al-Sham with her servant Maysara, on favourable terms.

content.heading: Narrative and sequence
content.body: On his return, the tradition says Khadijah was satisfied with the handling of her goods and with what Maysara observed. The biographical account then connects her interest in Muhammad ﷺ with an approach made through Nafisa bint Munya.

content.heading: Significance and lessons
content.body: Khadijah was his first wife and remained his wife until her death. The accounts present her as a vital ally and supporter at the beginning of the revelation; this central role should be distinguished from narrative details that vary.
